title: Re: Anthropic reveals $900B AI spending commitments ah...
text:
> The filing directly discloses for the first time that Anthropic has agreed $895.4bn in purchase commitments and lease agreements for computing power and infrastructure, of which $447.5bn is expected to be incurred before the end of 2030.

So $448 billion committed, with unclear cancellation terms, through the next ~48 months.

Clearly this will be rising over time, but even a naive division results in $10bn per month of compute spending.

That honestly doesn't seem so bad relative to some of the claims I've seen? Their Q3 revenue is about $5.6bn per month and it's rising. They have so much money in the bank waiting to be deployed that they get a billion dollars of interest per year. Investors are desperate to put more money into the company.

They spend a lot on compute, but rolling it up into cumulative spend numbers makes it sound scarier.

title: Re: Oracle files to sell $20B in new stock, bonds to f...
text:
Oracle does not have any proprietary IP that OpenAI depends on. That means Oracle is providing commodity services to OpenAI.

AI hardware is advancing rapidly. If NVIDIA's next generations deliver radically more tokens per watt and per dollar, an Oracle facility designed, financed, and contracted around an older GPU generation can be overtaken before it is fully online or fully monetized.

That's a big risk.

And to finance this they are making deep cuts to the ERP business where Oracle does have proprietary IP.

title: Re: Show HN: Intent-lens – see what Claude Code is abo...
text:
Hey HN. I use Claude Code in auto mode a lot and kept catching myself not reading the commands it runs. They scroll past fast, and half of them are find | xargs | awk one-liners I'd need a minute to parse anyway

So I made a small plugin that puts one plain line above the prompt while the call is running, like "Survey disk usage by file type", and for longer pipelines it spells out the steps. If the command looks destructive (rm -rf, force push, curl | sh, that kind of thing) the line goes red and you get a warning for a few seconds

It works off the tool's own arguments, so by default there's no extra model call and nothing leaves your machine. There's an optional mode where it asks Claude to reword the unclear ones, mostly edits

The risk check is just pattern matching on the command text, so think of it as a heads-up, not a safety net

Curious what else you'd want it to catch

title: Show HN: Hanging Context – news by an agent, for other agents
text:
Back in 2022 I was building a data and news site for family offices, private wealth and investment managers. We used the early OpenAI models to write data-driven stories covering the markets for art, collectibles, luxury goods and other cultural assets.

Mid-2024, a well-known AI company asked to license our stories. The big labs were signing licensing deals with media companies.

This is when it clicked. The biggest reader of news wasn’t going to be people. It was going to be their agents, and agents have unlimited hours of attention.

So I built Synorb. It reads thousands of sources and turns fresh content objects into Manifests (structured claims with provenance) that are dispatched via Streams anchored to organizations, people and datasets.

Hanging Context is an experiment on top of that. Could an agent read our streams and stand up a news site for other agents to read and find trustworthy?

The first version with a home-brewed Hermes agent was cumbersome so I tried Instinct and Muse when they released and settled on Muse as I found it better at narratives, images.

An agent runs the site. I wrote this post.

How it works:

Every 12 hours Muse reads hundreds of new Manifests published in our streams, then writes a new edition for the site. Every article produced cites the Manifests it used.

Before it publishes an article, an API checks it for quotes. They must appear word for word in a cited Manifest. Every paragraph needs to be backed by a citation and sources have to be under 24 hours old.

Muse doesn’t probabilistically determine what to trust - if 3 or more different sources back it, it’s "Confirmed". Otherwise it’s "Reported". At the time of writing, the site had 30 of 45 articles Confirmed. Here’s an article with 3 sources cited; the panel at the bottom shows what was checked: https://hangingcontext.com/stories/2026-11-02/agent-stack-re...

It costs almost nothing to run as I'm using Muse on the free plan, and since it only needs to pull Manifests, reason and write, it can run just fine.

To try it, just add https://hangingcontext.com/mcp to Claude, Cursor or any MCP client. No sign-up or key required. Setup: https://github.com/Synorb/hanging-context.

What I’m trying to figure out:

When I saw the early pull numbers by agents, I thought this could be a lead-gen micro-site for Synorb. I’ve built those before for human focused consumer and enterprise products.

Conversion is now the challenge. For a casual daily read, Hanging Context already does all the work. I don’t want to be annoying and cut coverage or show previews. So my plan is to just keep it free and try grow the number of agents pulling daily.

Full Disclosure: Synorb is my paid product, and Muse reads through its own Synorb account.

Curious if your agents would trust news written by another agent and what I can do to improve the odds.

title: Re: Anthropic's internal AI use, at retail prices, now...
text: I'm not really sure I understand the excitement around this. It seems like the implication is that if retail price > employee salary, you are replacing employees with AI spend? author: JohnMakin

title: Re: Ginux Replacing Linux...
text:
Now ... the title is catchy and I will state upfront that Ginux is not about to replace Linux - at the least not anytime soon. But probably also not in the future, as the Linux kernel having a team of real human behind itself, is IMO a stronger foundation than a ChatGPT-created Operating System, such as Ginux.

Anyway - the article is still quite interesting.

"In 11 days, I built a new Linux-compatible operating system kernel that boots Rocky Linux 10 with systemd, all using Human-Directed Agentic Engineering (HDAE)."

This is quite interesting though. Imagine if it would take 11 days only, to replace all Top 500 supercomputers running Linux with Ginux or anything similar. Again, not saying this is likely right now but I think sooner or later this may happen. Or at the least "real" competition.

Of course Ginux right now is nowhere an equivalent:

"Ginux runs only in a QEMU virtual machine, with no physical hardware profile"

And solving the hardware problem is big; HaikuOS still struggles here, ReactOS even more.

But this is also a finite problem set; soone or later AI slop agents will have figured that out. And then it will become more interesting.

Personally I have no interest in AI-linux or AI-operating-systems, but you can see that omarchy slop built by DHH is popular (see distrowatch, it is on rank #11 or something like that; yes, that is only a partial view, but TIOBE is also only a partial view, but still not 100% rubbish, just ... 80% rubbish 20% interesting).

Of course peer review by humans is more important than self-promo description by the human creator of Ginux, but I think sooner or later that'll also be solved.

author: Zigurd

title: Re: Grokipedia offers lessons in how AI can help Wikip...
text:
tl;dr: "I wish my Wikipedia page was more detailed, therefore Wikipedia should adopt AI"

> Grok’s voracious internet searches sometimes find things that human editors don’t. The long article about me includes a substantive discussion of my research about lying in politics and my work with fact-checkers around the world, neither of which are in the Wikipedia version.

I.e., author is mad his wikipedia page doesn't portray him how he wants to be portrayed. At least insofar as the author doesn't get to dictate how his Wikipedia page frames him, this is working as intended. Maybe add some notes to the talk page about yourself if you want someone to take up the cause of glorifying your record more thoroughly.

> Grokipedia also provides some welcome balance. When it offers context, Grokipedia can be a little heavy with hype (“His work has been lauded for innovating transparency in media…”) But it also included a “Criticisms and Controversies” section that details complaints that PolitiFact is biased against Republicans. That section has a healthy back and forth about the critiques and my response. That kind of balance could be helpful for Wikipedia, which has taken heat from Musk and others for being too lefty.

I.e., Wikipedia has higher standards for what to include. Working as intended.

> Musk’s encyclopedia also has a playful spirit that Wikipedia could learn from. Grokipedia’s homepage features random samples of recent edits that provide a glimpse at how the site is being improved. Another Grokipedia feature reads articles aloud in an AI voice you select: Eve, who sounds like a BBC anchor; Ara, a serious woman with crisp diction; Leo, who might have been a professor at Oxford; and Sal, whose name suggests a sports bar but whose voice is NPR.

This really has nothing to do with Wikipedia's concerns about AI-generated edits to articles.

> My big takeaway from Grok is the importance of human judgment in curating knowledge. Grok is a bot trying to behave like a human editor. Its many mistakes and lousy writing show that AI is not ready to replace Wikipedia’s talented volunteers. Still, Grok shows that AI can be a tool that helps them research and write better articles.

None of the evidence described in the article suggests this conclusion.

> After seeing an AI encyclopedia up close through my experiences with Grok, I come away with hope. Yes, AI can be a sloppy researcher and an awful writer. But Grok’s performance, shaky as it was, highlighted AI’s readiness for higher-level responsibilities.

Literally contradicting the sentence before "AI can be a tool that helps them research and write better articles."
